description: Detect, contain, recover, notify, learn — your calm playbook for when something gets breached.

screens.body:
Here's the uncomfortable truth: most teams get breached eventually. The teams that survive aren't the ones with perfect defenses — they're the ones with a plan.

An incident response plan is just decisions made calmly in advance: who do we call, what do we shut down first, who talks to users.

As a dev, your version is simple: know your team's security contact, know where the "big red button" docs are, and never try to hide a breach.

options: Calm decisions now beat panicked ones later
check.question: Why plan for a breach in advance?

screens.heading: Assume breach: plan before panic
screens.keyPoint: Decide calmly now what you'll do in a crisis.

screens.body:
You can't respond to what you don't notice. Detection is learning your system's "normal" so "weird" stands out.

Weird looks like: logins at 3 AM from new countries, a sudden flood of password resets, users reporting things they didn't do.

This is why logging matters (see secure coding): good logs are your security cameras. Review alerts — an ignored alert is the same as no alert.

options: Dozens of failed logins for one account at 3 AM
A user changing their profile photo
check.question: Which is a sign worth investigating?

screens.heading: Detect: notice something's off
screens.keyPoint: Know your normal so weird stands out.

screens.body:
Once you confirm something's wrong, contain it: limit the damage before you fix the cause. Think tourniquet before surgery.

Containment moves: revoke leaked keys and tokens, force password resets, take the affected service offline or isolate it.

But don't destroy evidence — keep logs and snapshots. You'll need them to understand what happened (and to prove it later).

check.question: An API key leaks. What's the first containment move?

code.snippet:
// contain first, investigate second
revokeKey(leakedKey);     // stop the bleeding
snapshotLogs();           // preserve the evidence
isolate(affectedService); // limit the spread

screens.heading: Contain: stop the bleeding
screens.keyPoint: Contain first: revoke, isolate — but preserve evidence.

screens.body:
After containment, remove the actual cause: patch the bug, delete the attacker's access, close the door they used.

Then recover carefully: restore from a clean backup (one from before the breach), change passwords and keys, and watch closely for a return visit.

Rushing recovery is how teams get breached twice by the same hole. Verify the fix before you declare victory.

options: Remove the cause, then restore from a clean backup
Change the logo and move on
check.question: What's the right recovery order?

code.snippet:
// recover in order — no shortcuts
patch(theBug);        // close the door
restore(cleanBackup); // rebuild from before the breach
rotate(allKeys);      // fresh secrets everywhere
monitorClosely();     // watch for round two

screens.heading: Eradicate & recover: clean, then rebuild
screens.keyPoint: Remove the cause, restore clean, rotate secrets, watch.

screens.body:
Hiding a breach always ends worse than reporting it. Tell your team lead and security contact immediately — fast internal notice limits damage.

Users whose data was affected deserve to know: what happened, what data was involved, and what they should do (like change passwords).

In Canada, privacy law (PIPEDA) can require reporting serious breaches to the Privacy Commissioner and notifying affected people. When in doubt, escalate — don't decide alone.

options: Fast notice limits damage; hiding it makes everything worse
It's faster than fixing the bug
check.question: Why notify quickly instead of hiding a breach?

screens.heading: Notify: tell the right people
screens.keyPoint: Tell your team fast, tell affected users honestly.

screens.body:
After the dust settles, run a postmortem: a structured look at what happened, when, and what you'll change.

The key rule: blameless. If people fear punishment, they hide mistakes — and hidden mistakes repeat. Ask "how did our process allow this?" not "who messed up?"

Write it down: timeline, root cause, and concrete fixes with owners. A postmortem nobody reads is just a diary.

options: Blame makes people hide mistakes, so they repeat
check.question: Why must postmortems be blameless?

screens.heading: Learn: the blameless postmortem
screens.keyPoint: Blameless review: fix the process, not the person.

screens.body:
Five steps, in order — tape this to your monitor:

1. Detect — notice the weird.
2. Contain — revoke, isolate, preserve evidence.
3. Eradicate & recover — fix the cause, restore clean.
4. Notify — team first, affected users honestly.
5. Learn — blameless postmortem with real fixes.

You won't remember this perfectly mid-crisis. That's the point of the plan: future-panicked-you just follows the steps.
screens.heading: Your incident playbook
screens.keyPoint: Detect, contain, recover, notify, learn — in that order.
